discovery: Squeezed light for surpassing the quantum shot-noise limit in gravitational-wave interferometry
motivation: Caves showed in 1981 that the quantum noise of a laser interferometer comes from vacuum fluctuations entering its dark port, and that injecting squeezed vacuum could beat the supposedly fundamental shot-noise limit. It took three decades of experimental work to make this real at audio frequencies, where gravitational-wave detectors operate. Mavalvala and Schnabel led that work. They produced stable squeezed vacuum at low frequencies, controlled its phase, and cut optical losses enough for it to be injected into kilometre-scale detectors. GEO600 used squeezing from 2010 onward. Squeezing has improved sensitivity in LIGO and Virgo in every observing run since O3, and frequency-dependent squeezing now lowers quantum noise across the whole detection band. More black-hole and neutron-star mergers are detected because of it. This is the first time engineered quantum states have improved a working astronomical observatory, and it underlies quantum-enhanced sensing more broadly.
